extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, literary students, and critics interested in narrative method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on narrative method for writing and evaluating novels, especially the choice between panoramic (pictorial) and scenic (dramatic) treatments, handling of point of view, preparation of characters for climactic revelation, and uses of time and authorial presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show characters from multiple viewpoints
rubrics_metrics.description: “Her relation to her husband... advantages in seeing it from his side too.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, present important characters from more than one vantage point (their own view and others' views). Doing so makes the character more solid, integrates them into the circle of other characters' experience, and can intensify later revelations (example: showing Emma from her own side and from Charles's point of view).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare characters' inner life in advance for later effects
rubrics_metrics.description: “Charles must be held in readiness... his inner mind, and his point of view, must be created in advance and kept in reserve, so that the force of the climax... may be instantly felt.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a character is needed to produce a climactic emotional or ironic effect later, build that character's inner life and viewpoint earlier in the narrative so the later disclosure feels earned and immediate (example: Charles's early episodes prepare his belated discovery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame the main story with a complementary affair
rubrics_metrics.description: “The whole book... is effectively framed in this other affair, that of Charles, in which it opens and closes.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider opening/closing or otherwise framing your principal narrative with a secondary or contrasting storyline. A framing affair can give structure, symmetry, and perspective to the central plot and help balance focus among characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict variety of method to the story's bare needs
rubrics_metrics.description: “With its variety of method, and with its careful restriction of that variety to its bare needs...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple narrative techniques (summary, scene, retrospection, authorial comment) only as required by the material. Superfluous shifts dilute effect; controlled variation serves clarity and unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose deliberately between panoramic (pictorial) and scenic (dramatic) presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: “Distinction between the ‘panoramic’ and the ‘scenic’ presentation of a story...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the novel's primary aim is to present a broad impression of a society/period (panorama/picture) or to enact particular events and confrontations directly (scene/drama). The choice should follow what the story requires (examples: Thackeray = panoramic, Maupassant = scenic).

rubrics_metrics.name: For panoramic works, build unity through typicality and impression rather than intricate plot
rubrics_metrics.description: “The unity... depends in truth upon one fact only, the fact that all his throng of men and women are strongly, picturesquely typical of the world from which they are taken.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing a broad, panoramic novel, focus on creating characters and episodes that together form a representative impression of a milieu; unity arises from the combined effect of types and atmosphere rather than a tightly woven plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge and manage authorial presence in panoramic narration
rubrics_metrics.description: “Thackeray cannot be the nameless abstraction... he must be present to the reader as a narrator and a showman.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panoramic/pictorial narration naturally foregrounds the narrator's voice. Use that presence consciously—as commentary, tonal shaping, or organizing intelligence—while bearing in mind how it affects reader relation and perceived authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use brief incidents, hints, and memory-flashes to enrich panoramas
rubrics_metrics.description: “A hint, a moment, a glance suffices... the little incident shows itself and vanishes.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In panoramic writing, accumulate brief, evocative moments rather than sustained scenes. These flashes and glimpses illustrate and enrich the general impression without halting the panoramic flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enact climactic or decisive scenes directly rather than summarizing them
rubrics_metrics.description: “The final scene ... must be placed immediately before us... The best possible... will be the plain and immediate performance of the answer, its embodiment in a scene that shall pass directly in front of us.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the narrative reaches a crucial turning point or decisive moral/emotional test, present it as a full, immediate scene so the reader can judge events directly rather than through retrospective summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare dramatic scenes in advance to avoid artificial theatricality
rubrics_metrics.description: “He neglected it in advance... he refused it till the last possible moment... he is forced to use devices of some crudity—because his climax... has been insufficiently prepared for.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you intend to switch from panoramic narration to an enacted climax, prepare characters and relationships early so that when the scene is acted out it feels natural. Failure to prepare leads to forced or 'crude' devices and an unconvincing theatrical tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not expect characters to perform a climax without earlier rendering
rubrics_metrics.description: “A little too much is expected of them, and they must make an unnatural effort to meet it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on a sudden shift that demands greater dramatic presence of characters than their prior development allows; give them the rendering and agency beforehand so their actions in crucial scenes are credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use intense memory-flashes sparingly—recognize their fragmentary limits
rubrics_metrics.description: “These flashes of revelation... are all the drama, strictly speaking, that he extorts from his material. The rest is picture.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memory-flashes can produce moments of high intensity, but they are fragments and do not substitute for sustained enactment when the story requires continuous dramatic action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulate chronology and focus in panoramas to create a sense of time
rubrics_metrics.description: “By what leisurely play with the chronology of the story, apparently careless and unmethodical, or by what shifting of the focus... Time, at Castlewood, is not movement, it is tranquillity.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panoramic narratives often use non-linear chronology, revisits, and shifts of focus to convey layered, 'stored' time rather than chronological movement. Use these devices to evoke the quality of time appropriate to place and mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether the reader should 'listen' to the narrator or 'watch' the story
rubrics_metrics.description: “In one case the reader faces towards the story-teller and listens to him, in the other he turns towards the story and watches it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly choose the reader's relation to the text: a confiding narrator (listener mode) shapes interpretation and tone; a dramatic, scenic presentation (watcher mode) asks the reader to judge events themselves. Maintain consistency or deliberate variation with purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prudent with omniscient authorial knowledge and authority
rubrics_metrics.description: “By convention the author is allowed his universal knowledge... But still it is a convention, and a prudent novelist does not strain it unnecessarily.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when using omniscience, avoid unnecessary intrusions of authorial commentary or over-assertion of knowledge that distracts from the story. Restrain or justify narrator omniscience to preserve the novel's self-contained effect.
